64.title: The first martyr, 1606
64.hook: tradition says he sat through it repeating that the Lord's will is sweet; Sikhs remember him as the first martyr
64.howItsDone: On the anniversary of Guru Arjan's martyrdom in early summer, Sikhs gather for recitation and set up chhabeel stalls, handing out cold sweetened water to passersby.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the arrest at Lahore, and simran: the Guru who would not let Mian Mir plead for him. Your line was steady in the heat.

A blazing day in early summer, in Punjab or in a Sikh neighborhood far from it, and you're stopped on the road. Not by the police. By smiling people, often teenagers, holding out cups of cold, sweet water, sometimes milky and rose-pink. They hand one to every driver, every walker, every bus passenger, free, all day. It's called a chhabeel, and it looks like pure summer kindness. It is. But it's also a remembering: those cups are poured in memory of a man who was tortured in the summer heat.
screen: `STOPPED ON A HOT ROAD.` → `COLD SWEET WATER, FREE.` → `A KINDNESS THAT REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Shaheed: a martyr. The word came into Punjabi from Arabic, where its root means a witness, someone who sees and testifies. A shaheed is a witness who gives their life rather than give up what is true. Sikhs call Guru Arjan the first Sikh shaheed, and the story of how he died is why. Tradition says that after days of torture in the Lahore heat, he asked to bathe in the river Ravi, which ran beside the fort. He walked into the water and was never seen again. In 1606, on a summer day, the fifth Guru was gone. Through it all, tradition says, he kept repeating a line from one of his own hymns. It's in the Guru Granth Sahib, and it says, roughly: whatever you do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. Your will is sweet. Not because pain is sweet. Pain is pain, and the torture was a crime. Sikhs read it as trust in God so deep that even this did not make him curse anyone. And look at what his community did with his death. They didn't turn it into a revenge story. On his martyrdom day, Sikhs recite, remember, and set up those roadside stalls of sweet water for anyone who is thirsty. A man who suffered in the heat, remembered with a cup of cold water held out to a stranger.

65.title: Two swords
65.hook: the young sixth Guru wears two swords, one for worldly duty and one for the spirit
65.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Hargobind's two swords of miri and piri as the ideal of the saint-soldier, and the two curved swords of the Khanda emblem on the Sikh flag are often explained as miri and piri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shaheed: a witness, and Guru Arjan, the first Sikh martyr. Your line was your will is sweet.

Picture the boy. His name is Hargobind, he's about eleven, and his father has just been killed in Lahore. Now he is the sixth Guru, and the whole community is watching him, grieving and frightened. What will he be? Up to now the Gurus have carried no weapons. They've been teachers, poets, builders of pools and kitchens. On the day he is formally installed as Guru, old Baba Buddha, the man who read the first hukam, brings out the things a Guru is given. And the boy asks for something new. A sword. Then a second one.
screen: `A BOY OF ABOUT ELEVEN.` → `HIS FATHER KILLED IN LAHORE.` → `A SWORD, THEN A SECOND.`

segments.voice: Two words, two swords. Miri comes from mir, the Persian word for a ruler or commander: worldly authority, the business of protecting people and running things. Piri comes from pir, a spiritual guide: spiritual authority, the inner life, the Name. Guru Hargobind wore one sword for each, on either side. His meaning was plain. After what happened in Lahore, faith would not be defenseless. The Guru would still be a guide of souls, and also a leader who could protect his people. He began to keep horses and train fighters, and Sikhs were asked to bring weapons and horses as offerings along with everything else. Here's what's easy to miss. The two swords were not two separate lives, a religious one on Sunday and a practical one the rest of the week. Sikhs understand the point as the opposite: the worldly sword must be guided by the spiritual one. Power without the Name becomes cruelty; the Name without care for the world can walk away from people who are suffering. Many Sikhs describe the ideal as saint and soldier in one person. You can still see the two swords today. The Khanda, the emblem on Sikh flags, has a double-edged blade in the center, and on either side curves a sword, often explained as miri and piri. Two swords. One heart holding them.

segments.voice: If you can, stand tall for thirty seconds: feet under your hips, spine long, shoulders down, chin level. Feel both hands at your sides, one holding what you have to take care of, work, bills, people who depend on you, the other holding the quiet center you come back to. Then sit, and keep that same tallness, both sides held together.
Miri piri. Worldly authority and spiritual authority, worn by Guru Hargobind as two swords, the spirit guiding the world.

66.title: The throne of the timeless
66.hook: he raises a platform facing the Harmandir, where the community meets on worldly matters
66.howItsDone: The Akal Takht in Amritsar is the foremost of the five takhts, the seats of Sikh temporal authority, and decisions and edicts for the Sikh community are issued from there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, miri piri: two swords, the spirit guiding the world. Your line was two swords, one heart.

In the world Guru Hargobind grew up in, one throne counted: the emperor's. He sat high, and his word was law. Under him, governors sat on smaller thrones, and so on down; everyone knew who was above them. Now the young Guru, wearing his two swords, does something bold. Right across from the Harmandir Sahib, facing its door, he builds a raised platform. A seat where he holds court, receives visitors, hears disputes and talks over the community's worldly affairs. And he gives it a name that answers the question of whose throne counts.
screen: `ONE THRONE THAT COUNTED.` → `A PLATFORM FACING THE HARMANDIR.` → `WHOSE THRONE IS IT?`

segments.voice: Takht means throne. Akal means timeless, beyond death, beyond time; you met it in the Mool Mantar: Akal Moorat, the timeless form. So the Akal Takht is the throne of the Timeless One, God's own throne. Not the Guru's, and certainly not any emperor's. Sikh tradition says the Guru built it in 1606 with Baba Buddha and Bhai Gurdas, and no hired laborers, just the Guru and his Sikhs. Look at where it stands, because the placement is the teaching. The Harmandir sits low in the middle of the pool, the house of the Name, of singing and remembering: piri. The Akal Takht faces it, where the community meets about worldly matters, justice, defense, decisions: miri. Two buildings looking at each other, the spirit and the world in conversation, each keeping the other honest. Tradition says that at the Harmandir the Guru would listen to hymns, and at the Takht he would sit as a leader, hear news, and review his horsemen. The Akal Takht still stands, and still matters. Sikhs count it first among the five takhts, the seats of authority in Sikh life, and from there decisions are announced to Sikhs everywhere. Its name makes a quiet claim: no earthly throne is final. Only the timeless one.

67.title: The cloak with fifty-two tassels
67.hook: released from Gwalior fort, tradition says he left only if fifty-two imprisoned princes could come, holding his cloak
67.howItsDone: Each autumn Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, remembering Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior with the fifty-two princes; gurdwaras, especially the Harmandir Sahib, are lit with lamps and lights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One. Your line was the timeless throne.

You've been locked up a long time, months, maybe years. Then one morning the guard comes with news: the emperor has ordered your release. The gate is right there. But look around the cells. There are other prisoners here, dozens of them, held for politics, forgotten, with no one coming for them. The order says nothing about them. Only you. Sikh tradition tells what Guru Hargobind said when that order came to him in the fort at Gwalior. It's a story that ends with lamps.
screen: `YOU'RE FREE. GO.` → `THE OTHERS IN THEIR CELLS.` → `WHAT DID THE GURU SAY?`

segments.voice: Some time after he built the Akal Takht, Guru Hargobind was imprisoned by the emperor Jahangir in the great fort at Gwalior. Why, and for how long, the sources don't agree: some point to an unpaid fine left over from his father's case, some to the Guru's growing army, some to court enemies. Historians still argue over the dates. What Sikhs remember is how it ended. In the fort, tradition says, were fifty-two princes, rajas from the hill kingdoms, held as political prisoners, and the Guru befriended them. When the order came to free him, he refused to go alone: let these princes come too. The emperor, tradition says, answered with a clever condition: as many as can hold on to your cloak as you walk out. Tradition says he expected only a few. So the Guru had a cloak made with fifty-two long tassels, one for each prince, and out through the gate they walked, all fifty-two, each holding a tassel. For this, Sikhs call him Bandi Chhor, the one who frees the prisoners. Tradition says he reached Amritsar around the time of Diwali, and the city lit lamps to welcome him. That's why each autumn, while Hindus celebrate Diwali, Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the day of release, and the Harmandir Sahib glows with lights and fireworks over the water. One man's freedom, stretched wide enough for fifty-two.

68.title: Home to the hills
68.hook: after battles with Mughal forces, Guru Hargobind settles at Kiratpur and spends his last years quietly
68.howItsDone: Kiratpur Sahib on the Sutlej, where Guru Hargobind spent his last years, is a place of Sikh pilgrimage, and some Sikh families today take the ashes of their loved ones there to be scattered in the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cloak with fifty-two tassels, and Bandi Chhor: the prisoners who walked out holding on. Your line was no one freed alone.

Some people never learn to stop. The firefighter who can't sit through dinner without listening for the siren. The parent who, years after the kids leave, still sleeps with one ear open. The soldier who comes home and can't find the off switch. Guru Hargobind spent most of his life on guard: a boy Guru after his father's killing, two swords, an army, a prison fort, and in his later years, real battles. Then he went up into the foothills and did something his whole life had not trained him for. He rested.
screen: `PEOPLE WHO NEVER STOP.` → `A LIFE ON GUARD.` → `THEN, THE FOOTHILLS.`

segments.voice: In the years around 1634, the peace between the Guru and the Mughal authorities broke down. Tradition tells of several clashes; one began, the story goes, with a dispute over a hunting hawk. Sikh accounts count four battles, in and around Amritsar and further south, and say that in each the Guru's small force held its own against much larger ones. Sikhs remember these as the first battles fought by a Guru. In one, the Guru's own youngest son, a boy named Tyag Mal, fought so hard he earned a new name; that's a story for day seventy-four. But the Guru did not want endless war. After the last battle, at Kartarpur near the Beas river, he led his family and followers north into the Shivalik foothills, to a town on the Sutlej river called Kiratpur. His son Baba Gurditta had founded it on land given by a hill raja. It was quiet, green, out of the way. There, tradition says, for about his last ten years, Guru Hargobind lived peacefully. He kept horses and a hunting ground, but the fighting was over. He preached, received visitors, looked after his community, and prepared the next Guru, passing over his sons to choose a grandson, Har Rai, a gentle boy of about fourteen. Guru Hargobind died at Kiratpur in 1644. The Guru who first wore two swords put them down. Sikhs read miri piri as a balance, not a call to fight forever, and at Kiratpur the balance tipped toward rest.

Kiratpur. The town in the Shivalik foothills where Guru Hargobind spent his last ten years in peace, after years of battles.

69.title: The flower and the robe
69.hook: tradition says the boy Har Rai brushed a flower with his robe, broke it, and was told to walk gently all his life
69.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, for his gentleness and love of nature, and the story of the flower and the robe is often told to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kiratpur: Guru Hargobind's quiet last years in the hills. Your line was even warriors rest.

You've probably done it. Rushing through a doorway with a bag on your shoulder and knocking a glass off the counter. Catching someone's elbow with your backpack on the train. Walking through a garden and realizing, too late, that you've stepped on the one flower about to open. Nobody meant anything. You were just moving through the world a little too big, a little too fast. Tradition says it happened once to a boy at Kiratpur, the grandson Guru Hargobind would choose as the next Guru, and that what his grandfather told him shaped the rest of his life.
screen: `KNOCKING THE GLASS OFF.` → `TOO BIG, TOO FAST.` → `A BOY IN A GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Here is the story as Sikhs tell it. The boy Har Rai was walking through the garden at Kiratpur in a long, flowing robe. As he passed a flowering bush, the edge of his robe caught the flowers and broke them, and the petals fell to the ground. He stopped, upset. His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, saw it happen, and didn't scold him. Tradition says he told him gently: if you wear a flowing robe, you must learn to carry it carefully, so it doesn't harm the things around you. The boy took it to heart. For the rest of his life, it's said, Har Rai walked holding his robe close, careful of flowers. That's the whole story. It's tiny, and it turned into a way of life. Har Rai became the seventh Guru, and Sikhs remember him above all for gentleness. He loved nature, and kept gardens and animals. Tradition says he kept horsemen, as his grandfather had, but never fought a battle. Read the robe as a picture of whatever gives a person size in the world: strength, voice, money, position, even a mood that fills a room. In the story the robe stays on; the boy learns to carry it close. The bigger the robe, the more carefully he walks. Sikhs see in the seventh Guru a picture of what power looks like when it is gentle.

70.title: The herb garden
70.hook: Guru Har Rai keeps a garden of medicines and sends a cure even to the emperor's son Dara Shikoh
70.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai for his herb garden and free medicines at Kiratpur, and many gurdwaras today run free clinics and medical camps in the same spirit of seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flower and the robe: Har Rai, the boy who learned to carry his size carefully. Your line was walk gently.

Someone from a family that has hurt yours gets sick. Not a stranger: the grandson of the man who ordered your great-grandfather's death, the son of the ruler whose soldiers fought your grandfather. His messengers come to your door. He's dying, and word is you have the medicine that could save him. Nobody would blame you for saying no. Plenty of people would blame you for saying yes. That was the choice in front of Guru Har Rai, the gentle seventh Guru.
screen: `A SICK MAN FROM THE OTHER SIDE.` → `HIS MESSENGERS AT YOUR DOOR.` → `YES, OR NO?`

segments.voice: At Kiratpur, Guru Har Rai kept a large garden of medicinal herbs, and a place where medicines were made and given out free. Healing was part of his gentleness: the boy who wouldn't break a flower grew into a man who used plants to mend people. The emperor Shah Jahan had a favorite son, Prince Dara Shikoh, the eldest, a scholar who loved the mystics of every tradition. Tradition says Dara fell dangerously ill, and the court physicians could find nothing to help. Word came that a rare remedy was kept in the Guru's store, and the emperor sent a request. This was the same royal family whose emperor Jahangir had ordered Guru Arjan's death, and whose forces had fought Guru Hargobind. The Guru sent the medicine, and tradition says Dara recovered. Tradition gives the Guru's reason in a picture: a tree does not ask who is throwing stones at it before it gives fruit, and it gives shade to the one who cuts it down. Heal whoever asks. Look back over the week: Guru Arjan, the first martyr, remembered with cold water for strangers. Two swords and a timeless throne. A cloak that freed fifty-two. A Guru who knew when to rest. A boy careful of flowers. And now a garden that heals the enemy's son. The thread is strength that won't turn bitter, and the Sikh story keeps saying it, week after week.

segments.voice: If there's a plant near you, go to it: water it, turn it toward the light, take off one dead leaf. If there isn't, picture one you know, a tree on your street, something on a windowsill, and look at it the way a gardener does, noticing what it needs. Then sit with it a while and breathe: something alive, being looked after.
